359.t: His grandparents' common sense and wartime stories
359.s: He grew up with all four grandparents, still consults them in his mind, and recalls his paternal grandfather's wartime hardships.
359.q: Yeah. I think so too you know. You know I grew up with my grandparents, all four of them. And they had a long life. So I was already an adult and still having four of them around. And there isn’t one single day that goes by without me thinking of my grandparents you know, and whenever I have to…

984.t: His father, Uncle Dick Mariani and the family
984.s: His parents met through Uncle Dick's band in 1936; he describes his father's background, alcoholism and switch to piano, and the Billy Kyle and Al Haig connection.
984.q: Dick Mariani, yeah, I think they had equal level of talent, which was, in my estimation a high level, both of them. So I’m not sure which side of the family I got the genes from, assuming I have any genes that are with musical talent. But I got it. Yeah, that’s how my mother met my father. My…

141.t: His mother's views, travels and grandmother Mom Ollie
141.s: Audre recalls his mother's remarks about Black labor, her world travels and his time at his grandmother's house.
141.q: Also, what about how you remembered what she said that time that made you feel proud of her when she was talking on the porch about how people made their money down there? She said “You all have to remember that what you made, you made from the sweat of their backs” or something like that. They…

490.s: He knows little of his father, who worked around gas stations and left the family.
490.q: I don’t know, really. My father – I think we worked in Gas stations and stuff, I think he might have been a mechanic, something like that.

368.t: Aunts Grace and Lucy and uncle Anthony raise the children
368.s: After the divorce the father's siblings, especially Aunt Grace, took care of the children.
368.q: Well, as it turned out my father had married twice, he had gotten a divorce from my mom. The one thing, they went through, unbelievable, the third act of Faust to get a divorce, you know. It was ridiculous what he had to go through because, there again, the family physician said that he should have…

142.t: His father after the revolution: army, theater, lost business
142.s: His father retired from the army, taught older people and played in a theater; when Castro took power his instrument business ended and the Paris study plan collapsed.
142.q: He retire from the army and teach older people, I think for free. You look around and all the old people, he was teaching them. And he played in the Teatro Marti; he used to play in the theater called Oh say Mariti Theater. It was a popular theater. So, I’m doing cabaret once in a while and he…

527.t: Parents' work, father's death, move to Phoenix
527.s: Little memory of Iowa; father died in a foundry accident, mother did foot care and teacher's help; the family moved to Phoenix after the parents separated.
527.q: [chuckles] Not really, ‘cause I was so young. When we moved, I was four. The recollections are like playing with the babysitter or something like that when I was just a little kid.

107.t: His parents' jobs, brother Charles and middle-class Walnut Hills
107.s: His father was a postal clerk and his mother a social worker and teacher; they lived on Stanton Avenue in Walnut Hills in a two-income middle-class family.
107.q: My father was a postal clerk. He worked -- this is the only job I’ve ever known him to hold, for my entire life, until he retired in his sixties. He was a postal clerk in the main post office in Cincinnati, Ohio, downtown Cincinnati.

144.t: Never knowing his father: the Detroit mosque photograph and his death
144.s: Fuller never knew his father, whose picture hung in the Detroit mosque. He knows little of his father's beliefs or Jamaican origin and was told he died of tuberculosis; he became self-contained.
144.q: I never knew him. There’s a picture of him in the mosque. I didn’t know anything about mosques or anything else at the time. There was a gentleman in the building named Mr. Briggs who told me about my father. “You’re just like him.”

328.t: Father as teacher: home schooling, expulsion from Virginia, and his death
328.s: His father taught the children, was run out of a Virginia town, read to them nightly, worked several jobs and died at 72.
328.q: A lot of the times, whenever we weren’t able to stay in one place and go to school, my dad was teaching us anyway, because he taught school. He actually taught public school. He was teaching in the South. He was teaching in the white school, but he reprimanded the mayor’s son once, and they ran us…

224.t: Family income and his parents' work
224.s: The family was middle class; his father bought a house and worked for Standard Oil, his mother did domestic work.
224.q: Middle class. When I was about two years old, my father bought a house there. I don’t know whether that was middle class, or what it was. They were immigrants. I think maybe at that time he was working for the Standard Oil company.

651.t: Working in the family florist business
651.s: How the florist began, who runs it now, his childhood chores, his choice of music over the business, and local deliveries.
651.q: I think my grandfather started a nursery business, and then my dad took it over, and they got into flowers. Weddings, funerals, things like that—general. Now my brother and his wife, they run it.

111.t: His father's work as a lumber inspector for General Motors
111.s: Elvin explains his father picked the lumber used in car and bus frames, and when the family left Vicksburg.
111.q: (Laughs) Well in the 20’s and the early 30’s most of the cars and busses and all that, they had wooden framework on the inside of the car. They had upholstery attached to that, and the steel would go over the top. So that was how cars were made .They used a lot of lumber and my Dad he was the one…

400.t: Growing up fatherless and his uncles' hotel-porter hustles that supported the family
400.s: Hinton resolved to keep his own family together; his uncles, hotel porters in Chicago, funded the apartment and slipped him secret dollars.
400.ch: Raising Charlotte and the extended family
400.q: Yeah watch me. And I felt that way having grown up without a father. I didn‟t have a father, you know since the time I was three months old. And I always said if I have a wife man, I am going to stick with her because I want them to have two parents. I am going to make that thing work, you know.…

672.t: Her household, siblings, grandparents and parents' work
672.s: Wilson describes her parents' divorce, father's remarriage, six children, many grandparents, and her parents' jobs; Mom is the stepmother, Mommy her mother.
672.q: My mother and father were married for about five or six years, and divorced. There was one – I had a brother. So they had two children. Then, when I was eight, my father remarried, and we had four more children. So I’m the oldest of six and lived with my father and his mother and father. In the…

953.t: Father's Navy friendship with Admiral Radford and the Harlem home
953.s: His proud career-Navy father was chagrined when Admiral Radford visited the family's crowded Harlem home.
953.q: Catfish Row. It’s sort of, you know, people all–and here comes my father, you know and here was Chief, you know, he called him Chief. And so he was a little bit, you know, and I think he chided my mother after that for not, you know, the place not, but I mean, you know, this is where we lived. This…

506.t: A family of eight children in Detroit
506.s: Carter describes his big family, his siblings' instruments, and how his father provided despite hard racial conditions.
506.q: I'm from a family of six girls and two boys. I'm in the middle, I guess. Several of them have passed away in the intervening years. I have a sister who plays piano and flute. I have a sister who played viola, one who played violin, who passed away. I'm the only one who decided to try to make a…

406.t: His father's death and his mother's insistence on school
406.s: His father died in 1921. He wanted to work to help support his siblings, but his mother made him stay in school, discovering his cement-plant job from the cement in his eyes.
406.ch: Carnivals, Kansas City and the road to Chicago
406.q: Anyway, Bill said, 'why don't you go to Chicago?' I said, 'well, man, I don't know how to' -- he said, 'Good as you play, you should be in Chicago.' So we decided that when he went back to Chicago I would go. So I didn't have money, you know, to go like that. Of course, I wanted to go for the very…

614.t: Father's shoe factory career and mother working the line
614.s: His father rose over 30 years to an executive in a shoe company, in charge of quality and styling, and his mother worked on a machine there to help the family income.
614.q: And my father was involved with a shoe factory, worked as an employee, and worked himself up over a period of 30 years to being an executive of that company.

68.t: Farm life and the city house
68.s: They lived on the farm until he was about 12, and the family had all it needed.
68.q: Yeah. Well, see, my father was a farmer that -- well, we raised everything like we had -- she had a beautiful garden and we just had about everything we needed, like meats and calves, you know, we had cows and we had everything we really needed. So I didn't have a hard time, you know, in that…

378.t: Mother's encouragement and urging to leave the small town
378.s: His mother told him to do what he wanted and wanted all her children out of Beardstown; the brothers left for college and never came back to live.
378.q: But I -- I really had a wonderful mother. She -- when my older brother used to rant and rave about me being a musician and all, she'd say, 'Well you gotta do what you gotta do. That's what you want to do, you do it.'

166.t: His mother defends the farm with pepper-loaded shells
166.s: His father was a rounder; his mother shot at chicken-thieving in-laws with hot-pepper loads.
166.ch: Family background and the Tulsa music scene
166.q: No, the only time I would hear him play would be on Sundays. But they all tried to run my mother off the farm, because my father was never home. He was a rounder, you know? And when he was away, his brothers would come up to the house and try to steal the horses, to ride into town at night and…

117.t: Neighbours complain about the idle Freeman boys
117.s: Neighbours pressure Freeman's father to make his sons work; he wakes them at 7:30 and Arnie protests, after which dad leaves them alone.
117.q: He just loved -- my father furthered all of this by wealth. There's a very funny story that goes along with it all. We lived in a community in Austin where people were always butting into other family's business and they had meetings. They noticed that my brother and I never did anything, because…

92.s: Collins lived with his godmother, a fair-skinned Montgomery pianist who worked as a governess and joined the post office in her sixties.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: Her name was Jesse Knight. She was from Montgomery, she was a very fair woman, very -- the red hair, long red hair, and her father was -- reminded me of Santa Claus. He had a flowing white beard, and he was -- well, he was white, you know, really. And when I went to New York I told you I stayed at…

93.t: Parents separate and move to Atlanta
93.s: The family leaves Fitzgerald when his father takes a niece away; Green and his mother go to his grandmother in Atlanta and his music lessons lapse.
93.q: Well, as I say, I cannot say years because only two years came, and then we had to leave Fitzgerald, Georgia. My parents didn't actually separate or divorce or anything, but they separated because my father had one of his brother's daughters there that he had been taking

418.t: Summer work for his father and his family in Xenia
418.s: He worked summers for his father's contracting business around Xenia, Springfield and Columbus; the storm that ruined the family house; his siblings.
418.q: Well, no, not during the holidays. Just a summer job, you know. ...(?)... to contract houses -- to plaster and all that, you know: that's what I was going to be.

388.t: Father's remarriage and living with grandparents in Portland
388.s: His father remarries around 1920 and builds a house nearby, but Leeman stays with his grandparents and goes through Portland schools.
388.q: No, I was still living with my grandparents, but it was an unusual setup because all this time, my father's business was going on, and my grandfather's was going on.

19.t: Moving to Washington: Deanwood, two rooms, repeating Fifth Grade at Garrison
19.s: His father goes ahead to find work, the family follows to Deanwood then cramped rooms in the city, and Malachi is held back a grade.
19.q: Anyway, my family stayed in Durham for...I guess we were there for, oh, practically five years. As I remember I was in the Fifth Grade, I think I was ten years old, and my father the year before had come to Washington to work, for the obvious reason -- first of all, work down there must have been…

125.t: Moving like gypsies and learning to make friends
125.s: The family moved every one to two years, forcing Thompson to make friends, sometimes through fights, and perhaps pushing him toward travelling music.
125.ch: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
125.q: Well, I think one of the most important things that was significant during that time, other than the things I've discussed already, was the amount of time we used to move as a family, of a minister. We moved so often it was almost like living the life of a gypsy throughout my early childhood. We…

171.t: Mother's laundry work and being the sickly youngest boy
171.s: His mother took in laundry and brought the children along; Ramey played on being the small, sickly baby boy.
171.q: Well, my mother was more or less a housewife, but she also did laundry, like that. And she took us with her. And we used to be so ashamed, you know. She'd take the three boys and my baby sister, when she went to washing in those people's back yards. We had to go, too. And that was an effort to be…
